subsection: 3. Urban settlement: site, hierarchy, hinterland and central place theory

notes.b: A town's site is the ground it is built on. The historic reasons for particular sites are covered in the note Viking longphorts and the first towns, and in the note Norman walled towns and manor villages.
points: Bridging point or ford: Dublin, on the Liffey, is the lowest bridging point on the river.
Route focus, where several roads meet: Athlone, at a crossing of the River Shannon in the centre of Ireland.
Island site: Limerick, on King's Island in the Shannon.
Sheltered harbour or estuary head: Waterford, on the Suir estuary, and Galway, at the mouth of the River Corrib.
Defensive sites on a hill, river loop or island, and dry points above wet ground.
Resources close to the site, such as water, fish, timber and stone.

notes.b: Situation is where the town lies in relation to the land and trade around it.
points: Centre of a fertile farming area, supplying goods to farmers and taking their produce.
On a coast facing trade partners, which gives access to sea routes.
At a gap through the uplands, where routes cross the high ground.
Residential, market and retail, and services such as health, education and administration.
Industrial, port and transport.
Tourism and recreation, ecclesiastical, defence or garrison.
Commuter (dormitory) towns, where most residents work elsewhere.
Most towns are multi-functional.

notes.b: Settlements are ranked by size and by the number and range of their functions and services.
points: The ranking runs from hamlet to village, small town, large town, city and capital (primate) city.
There are few large centres and many small ones, so the hierarchy takes the shape of a pyramid.
A place higher in the hierarchy has more functions and services, and draws people from a wider area.

notes.b: These are Census 2022 figures for cities and suburbs, and for towns.
points: Dublin: about 1.26 million people.
Regional cities: Cork, about 222,000; Limerick, about 102,000; Galway, about 86,000; Waterford, about 60,000.
Largest towns: Drogheda, about 44,000, which is Ireland's largest town; Dundalk, about 43,000; Swords, about 41,000. Swords is a town in Fingal, not a separate city.
Many smaller county and market towns, and villages. The State's population is about 5.1 million.

notes.b: A primate city is much larger than the second city in the country and dominates its functions.
points: Dublin is a primate city: about six times the size of Cork.
Causes of Dublin's primacy: its role as capital, its port, its routeway focus, colonial administration, multinational firms and services.
The rank-size rule, in which the nth city is one nth the size of the largest, does not fit Ireland.
The National Spatial Strategy and the National Planning Framework try to balance Dublin's growth with other centres. These are summarised in the note Urban planning and renewal.
Low-order goods are for convenience, such as bread and newspapers. They are found in every village, are bought often and have a low threshold.
High-order goods are comparison goods and specialised services, such as jewellers, department stores, hospitals and universities. They have a high threshold and are found only in large centres.

notes.b: The hinterland, also called the sphere of influence, catchment area or umland, is the surrounding area a town serves and draws people from.
points: The size of a hinterland depends on the town's size and functions, on transport, and on competition from nearby centres.
Newspaper circulation areas.
Bus routes and timetables.
Catchments of schools and hospitals.
Shop customer surveys and delivery areas.
Commuter flows.
Sports club catchments.
Hinterlands overlap and change.
Cars, motorways and online shopping widen hinterlands.
Bypasses and out-of-town centres change them.
Example: the large hinterland of Galway city across the West.

notes.b: Walter Christaller, a German geographer, published central place theory in 1933, based on a study of southern Germany.
points: A central place is a settlement providing goods and services to people in its surrounding area.
Threshold is the minimum number of customers needed to keep a service in business. It is a number of people.
Range is the maximum distance people will travel to obtain a service. It is a distance.
A service locates where its threshold falls within its range.
A flat, uniform (isotropic) plain.
An evenly spread population with equal purchasing power.
Equal ease of transport in all directions.
Consumers buy at the nearest centre.
No excess profits.
Market areas are hexagonal, because circles overlap or leave gaps and hexagons fit together.
A hierarchy of centres forms: many small, closely spaced low-order centres, and fewer, more widely spaced high-order centres.
Each higher-order centre also supplies all the lower-order goods.
Nesting: k = 3 is the marketing principle, k = 4 the transport principle and k = 7 the administrative principle.
In parts of the Irish Midlands, market towns serving farming areas are regularly spaced.
The Dutch polder Noordoostpolder, in the Netherlands, was drained in 1942. Emmeloord was planned as the central town, with ten villages around it, including Marknesse, Ens, Kraggenburg and Bant.
The villages were spaced so that farmers could reach one by bicycle. This gives a planned two-level hierarchy.
Relief, rivers and coasts are not uniform, and population is unevenly spread.
Transport routes are linear, not equal in all directions.
People shop on the way to work or on multi-purpose trips, not always at the nearest centre.
Car ownership, motorways, out-of-town shopping centres and online shopping change ranges and thresholds.
Government decisions, such as county towns and new towns, and history, such as Viking and Norman towns, fix locations.
Dublin's primacy breaks the regular hierarchy.
The theory was designed for market (service) towns, not for industrial, port or tourist towns.

notes.h: Applying central place theory to Ireland
points: Dublin is at the top, the regional cities come next, then county and market towns, then villages.
The Irish hierarchy is broadly hierarchical but distorted by Dublin's primacy and by the coastline.
Defence functions were lost.
Market and fair functions declined, as marts and supermarkets took over.
Industrial functions moved from the inner city to the suburbs or closed.
Services grew: offices, tourism, education and health.
Many towns near cities became commuter towns.
Village services such as the post office, Garda station, pub, shop and school have closed.

notes.h: Galway: Norman port and merchant town
points: Galway was a Norman town founded by the de Burgo family in the 13th century.
It was governed by 14 merchant families, the Tribes of Galway. A royal charter of 1484 was granted.
Galway traded wine with Spain and France.
The Spanish Arch, built in 1584, is a surviving part of the town walls.
Galway surrendered to Cromwellian forces in 1652, and a long decline followed.
Queen's College Galway was founded in 1845. It is now the University of Galway, renamed in 2022.
Digital Equipment Corporation opened a plant in Galway in 1971 and closed its manufacturing there in 1993.
Galway is now a centre of the medical devices industry, with multinationals such as Medtronic and Boston Scientific.
The National Spatial Strategy of 2002 named Galway a gateway. The National Planning Framework of 2018 aims for at least 50% growth in Galway by 2040.
Galway was European Capital of Culture in 2020, jointly with Rijeka, Croatia.
The Galway Arts Festival and the Galway Races at Ballybrit attract visitors.
Galway is the regional capital of the West.

notes.h: Limerick: walled city and Georgian port
points: Limerick began as a Viking settlement, covered in the note Viking longphorts and the first towns.
King John's Castle was built in the early 13th century on King's Island.
The Treaty of Limerick was signed in 1691.
Limerick developed as a Georgian commercial port. Its Georgian Newtown Pery is covered in the note Landlord and Georgian planned towns.
Limerick became an industrial city based on its port and flour milling.
Later industry linked to the Shannon area brought multinational investment. See the note Twentieth and twenty-first century settlement.
Dell opened in Limerick in 1990. In January 2009 it announced that it would move manufacturing to Łódź, Poland, with the loss of about 1,900 jobs.
The University of Limerick was founded in 1972 as the National Institute for Higher Education and became a university in 1989.
Limerick was Ireland's first National City of Culture, in 2014.
Limerick City and County Councils merged in 2014.
In 2024 Limerick elected Ireland's first directly elected mayor.

notes.b: Dublin's functions changed in stages. Its detail is in the note A Core Irish Region.
points: Viking trading port, covered in the note Viking longphorts and the first towns.
Administrative capital.
Georgian city, with the Wide Streets Commissioners of 1757 (see Landlord and Georgian planned towns).
Port and industry.
Services and technology in the Docklands: the International Financial Services Centre (1987), and Google at Grand Canal Dock.

notes.h: A market town becoming a commuter town
points: Market functions, such as the mart and shops serving farmers, decline as the town's population changes.
Services, housing and shops shift to serve commuters who travel to work in a larger city.
Commuter towns of the Greater Dublin Area include Navan, Ashbourne, Naas, Newbridge, Maynooth, Bray and Greystones.

notes.h: Reasons for the growth of an urban area
notes.b: Use this checklist with the Galway and Limerick case studies.
points: Site and situation: a bridging point, island, estuary or harbour.
Route focus and port: the town gathers traffic from roads, rivers or the sea.
Administrative role: a national capital, a regional capital or a merged council.
Industry and multinationals: manufacturing and foreign investment.
Services and education: universities and hospitals.
Tourism and culture.
Government policy: national gateways and growth targets, covered in the note Urban planning and renewal.
In-migration: people moving in for work and study.

keyTerms.definition: The ground a town is built on, such as a bridging point, island, estuary or defensive hill.
The position of a town relative to the farming area, coast, routes and uplands around it.
The ranking of settlements by size and by the number and range of their functions and services.
A city much larger than the second city in its country, dominant in its functions.
The surrounding area a town serves and draws people from.
A settlement that provides goods and services to people in its surrounding area.
The minimum number of customers needed to keep a service in business.
The maximum distance people will travel to obtain a service.
Goods bought often and found in every village, such as bread and newspapers.
Comparison goods and specialised services found only in large centres.
A town whose residents travel out to work, and whose services increasingly serve commuters.

questions.prompt: Examine central place theory with reference to examples you have studied.
questions.model: Walter Christaller published central place theory in 1933, based on a study of southern Germany. A central place provides goods and services to the people of its surrounding area. A service locates where its threshold, the minimum number of customers needed, falls within its range, the maximum distance people will travel. The theory assumes a flat, uniform plain, an evenly spread population with equal purchasing power, equal ease of transport in all directions, that consumers use the nearest centre, and no excess profits. It predicts hexagonal market areas, because hexagons fit together with no gaps, and a hierarchy of centres: many small, closely spaced low-order centres, and fewer, more widely spaced high-order centres. Each higher-order centre supplies all the lower-order goods. Nesting follows k = 3 for the marketing principle, k = 4 for the transport principle and k = 7 for the administrative principle. Evidence: market towns serving farming areas are regularly spaced in parts of the Irish Midlands, and the Dutch polder Noordoostpolder, drained in 1942, has Emmeloord as its central town with ten villages around it, spaced so farmers could reach one by bicycle. Applied to Ireland, Dublin sits at the top, the regional cities come next, then county and market towns, then villages. Limitations: relief, rivers and coasts are not uniform, and population is unevenly spread. Transport routes are linear. People shop on multi-purpose trips, not always at the nearest centre. Motorways, out-of-town shopping centres and online shopping change ranges and thresholds. Government decisions and history, such as Viking and Norman towns, fix locations. Dublin's primacy breaks the regular hierarchy, and the theory was designed for market towns, not for industrial, port or tourist towns.

questions.prompt: Examine how the functions of an urban centre have changed over time, with reference to one example you have studied.
questions.model: Galway. It was a Norman town founded by the de Burgo family in the 13th century, governed by 14 merchant families, the Tribes of Galway, and given a royal charter in 1484. Its walled port traded wine with Spain and France, and the Spanish Arch of 1584 is a surviving part of the town walls. Galway surrendered to Cromwellian forces in 1652, and a long decline followed. Queen's College Galway was founded in 1845, and is now the University of Galway, renamed in 2022. Digital Equipment Corporation opened a plant in Galway in 1971 and closed its manufacturing there in 1993. Galway is now a centre of the medical devices industry, with multinationals such as Medtronic and Boston Scientific. The National Spatial Strategy of 2002 named Galway a gateway. The National Planning Framework of 2018 aims for at least 50% growth in Galway by 2040. Galway was European Capital of Culture in 2020, jointly with Rijeka, Croatia. Its functions have moved from trade and defence, to education, high-tech manufacturing, tourism and culture, and it is the regional capital of the West.

questions.prompt: (i) Name one urban area you have studied. (ii) Name two of its functions. (iii) Describe and explain how its functions have changed over time.
questions.model: (i) Limerick. (ii) Two functions: port and industry, and education. (iii) Limerick began as a Viking settlement. King John's Castle was built in the early 13th century on King's Island, and the town was walled. The Treaty of Limerick was signed in 1691. In the late 18th century it developed as a Georgian commercial port, with Newtown Pery laid out. It became an industrial city based on its port and flour milling, and later multinational investment linked to the Shannon area brought new industry. The decline of older industry followed, and Dell announced in January 2009 that it would move manufacturing to Łódź, Poland, with the loss of about 1,900 jobs. The University of Limerick was founded in 1972 and became a university in 1989. Limerick was Ireland's first National City of Culture in 2014, and in 2024 it elected Ireland's first directly elected mayor. The functions moved from port and military defence, through industry, to education, culture and regeneration.
